headline: US cannabis taxes top $30 billion: where 23 adult-use states spend it
dek: A 27 November review of 23 adult-use states finds school, roads and Medicaid shares are clear, while equity and treatment money is often cut or untracked.
key_points: Combined US cannabis tax collections since 2014 now exceed $30 billion, according to a Marijuana Herald review of state records published on 27 November.
The Census Bureau estimates 30 states and DC collected $3.55 billion in cannabis excise tax between July 2025 and June 2026, up 15.7% from FY2022.
Several states have rewritten the original promises: Ohio now sends 64% to its general fund, Colorado ended a local share, and Maine and Minnesota trimmed dedicated funds.
Collections, appropriations and grant awards measure different things, and few states report what the money actually bought.
body: Legal cannabis has now produced more than $30 billion in state tax collections across the United States since sales began in 2014, but where that money ends up varies widely from state to state and is often hard to trace. That is the finding of a state-by-state review published on 27 November by The Marijuana Herald, which worked through government financial records, legislative audits, budgets and statutes in all 23 states with working adult-use markets.

The review leaves out Virginia, where retail sales are not due to begin until July 2027, as well as medical-only states and the District of Columbia. Its central warning is one operators and investors will recognise from budget fights in their own states: the headline promise made when a market opens is not always where the money goes years later.
## How big the pot has become

The most recent federal snapshot comes from the US Census Bureau, which published its estimates on 10 September. It found that 30 states and DC collected an estimated $3.55 billion in cannabis excise tax between July 2025 and June 2026, up 15.7% from $3.06 billion in fiscal 2022. When the bureau's quarterly survey began tracking the tax in 2021, 19 states and DC collected it. Alabama became the newest, with medical-only sales starting on 20 May 2026.

Per person, Washington and Montana lead the country, each collecting more than $50 per resident each year, with retail excise rates of 37% and 20%. Alaska collects more than $30 per resident without a retail excise tax, using a $50-per-ounce cultivation tax instead. Minnesota's collections roughly doubled to $34.44 million in fiscal 2026 from $16.57 million a year earlier after the state raised its rate from 10% to 15%. California shows the other side: its revenue fell from $878.56 million in fiscal 2022 to $528.23 million in fiscal 2023 after it ended its cultivation tax on 1 July 2022, the bureau said.

The Herald also cites a June report from the Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, which put state taxes from adult-use sales at about $28.4 billion from 2014 to the end of 2025, including a record $4.57 billion in 2025.
## Where the money is clearest

Washington offers the most detailed picture, thanks to a 2023 audit by its Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee covering $3.309 billion from fiscal 2015 to 2023. About 54%, or $1.803 billion, went to Medicaid health care for low-income children, and $1.009 billion went to the general fund. Prevention, education and treatment received $281.2 million; local governments $102.2 million; administration and enforcement $104.7 million; and research $8.4 million. The state's social equity programme received just $1.3 million, about 0.04%, after funding began in fiscal 2022, the Herald reported.

Michigan's split was written into its original law: 35% to K-12 schools, 35% to transportation and 30% to local governments and tribes. In fiscal 2025 that meant about $94 million to 313 local entities and tribes. A 24% wholesale tax that took effect on 1 January 2026 now sends nearly all its revenue to a Neighborhood Roads Fund, which the state transport department projected at about $420 million a year.

Missouri is the cleanest example of a fixed formula. After regulatory and expungement costs, recreational revenue is split equally between the Veterans Commission, the State Public Defender and addiction treatment. That came to about $58.9 million in fiscal 2026, or about $19.6 million each, and $128.6 million in cumulative recreational transfers by June 2026, according to the review.
> The tax that sold legalization to voters is now a budget line like any other, and legislatures are treating it that way.
## Promises that were rewritten

Ohio is the starkest case. When voters approved Issue 2 in November 2023, the fiscal analysis set out 36% for social equity and jobs, 36% for host communities, 25% for addiction services and 3% for regulation. Under current state law, the Herald found, 64% now goes to the general revenue fund and 36% to host communities, and the social equity and addiction shares are no longer in the formula.

Colorado has also cut local governments out. A June law, HB26-1409, ends the 3.5% share of retail sales tax that went to local governments from 1 July, after an earlier cut from 10%, and sends excess balances in its Marijuana Tax Cash Fund to the State Public School Fund. Colorado's cumulative state marijuana tax and fee collections reached about $3.28 billion through September 2026. Maine cut the dedicated public health and municipal share from 12% to 9% from 1 January 2026, and Minnesota repealed its local government cannabis aid in 2025 while raising its gross receipts tax to 15%.
Connecticut is moving the other way, raising the social equity share to 70% for fiscal 2027 and 2028, with a scheduled rise to 75% in fiscal 2029.
## Treatment and equity money: hard to measure

Oregon sends the largest share of its distributions to addiction services under Measure 110: $536.6 million to the Drug Treatment and Recovery Services Fund from January 2021 to June 2026, about two-thirds of $804.3 million distributed. But yearly payments to that fund fell from $131.4 million in 2021 to $80.7 million in 2025, a drop of about 39%, and a December 2025 audit by Oregon's Secretary of State found the health authority lacked the information to judge what the money achieved, the Herald reported.

Massachusetts sets aside 15% of prior-year Marijuana Regulation Fund revenue for a social equity trust fund and has awarded about $57.1 million over three fiscal years, with awards rising from 50 in fiscal 2024 to 194 in fiscal 2026. Illinois reports about $1.594 billion through its Cannabis Regulation Fund since fiscal 2020, with $652.2 million each to statewide budget support and to community reinvestment and services. The review notes these are grants and transfers, not verified spending.
## What it means for the industry

For operators, the pattern matters because tax revenue is the industry's main political argument. When the money flows into general funds or roads, it is easier for lawmakers to raise rates, as Minnesota, Maryland and Michigan have done, and harder for the industry to point to visible public benefits. The Census figures also show how sensitive collections are to tax design: California lost about 40% of its excise revenue in a single year when one tax was removed.
This comes as revenue is already under pressure. As we reported on 26 November, Whitney Economics found that 24 states saw cannabis revenue fall in 2025, up from 16 the year before.
## What to watch

State budget sessions in early 2027 are the next test. Watch for further rate rises or formula changes in states facing deficits, Virginia's tax design ahead of July 2027 sales, and whether more states follow Washington in publishing audits of what cannabis money buys. The next quarterly Census figures will show whether the 15.7% growth since fiscal 2022 holds as prices fall.
